CONFIRM C0083 — `_classify_event()` still classifies `MERGE C0001 <- F...` incorrectly because it searches for the literal substring `MERGE {finding_id}` in JSON text. In this codebase’s structured verdict syntax, the canonical target precedes `<-`, so merge detection is semantically tied to the target finding ID and should remain in the registry as an event-classification bug.

EXTEND C0083 | FOLLOW: `_describe_event()` depends on `_classify_event()`, so any merge misclassification propagates into provenance detail text as “submitted” instead of “merged”. `trace_finding()` therefore yields incomplete lifecycle traces for findings that are only referenced via MERGE verdicts, which is a HIGH correctness issue for reviewer-facing provenance.

DESCRIPTION: FIND: In `bench/evidence.py`, `EvidenceStore.trace_finding()` is documented and advertised as chronological provenance (“ordered sequence of events”, “chronological provenance trace”), but the implementation returns events in record-index order, not timestamp order. Evidence: it fetches `indices = self._index.by_finding.get(...)`, then iterates `for i in sorted(indices):`, appending events without any timestamp sort. `sorted(indices)` sorts chain positions only. In the underlying chain interface, timestamps are claimed wall-clock UTC strings supplied at append time and are not guaranteed to be monotonic with append order; `verification_chain.py` explicitly states the chain proves insertion order, not timestamp accuracy or timeliness. Therefore a later-appended backdated record will appear after newer timestamps, violating the chronological contract.
FOLLOW: This directly affects reviewer-visible provenance traces, causing silently wrong temporal ordering. Downstream, any consumer that interprets `trace_finding()` as lifecycle order may infer incorrect causal sequence between submission, challenge, confirm, checkpoint, and report events. `_describe_event()` itself is unaffected, but its outputs become misleading because they are attached to the wrong position in the sequence. This also weakens exported evidence review workflows if they rely on `trace_finding()` before choosing bundle contents.

FINDING_ID: F002

FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.56
DESCRIPTION: FIND: In `bench/evidence.py`, `EvidenceStore.export_bundle()` computes inclusion proofs against the current full chain regardless of whether the bundle’s `merkle_root` names an earlier sealed epoch. Evidence from code: each proof is built via `self._chain.build_inclusion_proof(i)`, and `VerificationChain.build_inclusion_proof()` always constructs the proof over `self._records` (the full current record set) and embeds that full-chain root in `proof["merkle_root"]`. But `export_bundle()` then sets `merkle_root = epochs[-1]["merkle_root"]` whenever any epoch exists. In `verification_chain.py`, `seal_epoch()` is not auto-called on append, so a chain can have a latest sealed epoch covering only a prefix of current records. In that normal state, proofs for records after the epoch are bound to the full-chain root while the bundle root is the older epoch root, so `verify_bundle()` will fail. Even records within the sealed prefix are emitted with proofs containing the full-chain root, and `verify_inclusion_proof()` explicitly rejects proofs whose embedded root differs from the supplied bundle root.
FOLLOW: This breaks the core advertised feature “Evidence bundle export — self-contained bundles with inclusion proofs” on active chains after additional appends post-seal. `verify_bundle()` will report false negatives for valid records, making exported bundles unusable for external audit. `chain_metadata["epoch_count"]` and `bundle.merkle_root` then describe a sealed epoch, while `inclusion_proofs` describe a different tree, so the bundle is internally inconsistent. Any UX or CLI built on bundle export/verify will mislead the reviewer about proof validity.

FINDING_ID: F003
SEVERITY: 0.83
FLAW_CLASS: 4
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.44
DESCRIPTION: FIND: In `bench/evidence.py`, `trace_finding()` only returns records whose `finding_id` was indexed into `by_finding`, but `_classify_event()` contains explicit logic for artifact types `health_scan`, `policy_snapshot`, `experiment_checkpoint`, and `experiment_report`. Evidence: `trace_finding()` starts with `indices = self._index.by_finding.get(finding_id, [])` and returns early if empty. The index only includes `rec.finding_ids`, which are extracted from payload content in `EvidenceRecord.from_chain_record()`. For records like `policy_snapshot`, there is typically no finding ID in payload; `_describe_event()` for `policy` even emits generic text without using payload content. So the provenance API claims “full lifecycle” / “every event related to this finding ID” but structurally cannot include contextual records from the same round/model unless they literally mention the finding ID. This is an implementation/documentation mismatch visible from the code alone.
FOLLOW: Provenance traces are incomplete by construction. The specific downstream gap is cross-referencing: module docstring item 3 promises linking a finding record to the active policy and health scan from that round, but `trace_finding()` never performs that join. Reviewers using provenance to audit why a verdict occurred will miss policy/health context even though helper classification/description code suggests such events belong in the trace. This is a HIGH completeness issue because it silently omits context the module explicitly advertises.
